Rotations, poses and Lie groups

Source: vignettes/spatial-math.Rmd
spatial-math.Rmd
library(robotcompR)

Every robotics computation rests on a handful of conventions. Mixing them silently is the most common source of wrong results, so robotcompR fixes one set and checks it wherever it can.

Rotation matrices

A rotation matrix R \in SO(3) satisfies R^\top R = I and \det R = 1. Rotations are active: R p rotates the vector p. The elementary rotations are

R_z(\theta) = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta & 0 \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}. 

rotz(pi / 2) %*% c(1, 0, 0)
#>              [,1]
#> [1,] 6.123234e-17
#> [2,] 1.000000e+00
#> [3,] 0.000000e+00
is_rotation_matrix(rotz(0.3) %*% rotx(0.2))
#> [1] TRUE

Numerical drift accumulates when many rotations are multiplied. orthonormalize() projects back onto SO(3) with the polar decomposition:

R <- diag(3)
for (i in 1:1000) R <- R %*% rotx(0.001) %*% roty(0.002)
max(abs(crossprod(R) - diag(3)))
#> [1] 5.451195e-14
R <- orthonormalize(R)
max(abs(crossprod(R) - diag(3)))
#> [1] 2.220446e-16

Euler angles

Sequences are intrinsic: "ZYX" means rotate about z, then about the new y, then about the newest x, so R = R_z(\alpha) R_y(\beta) R_x(\gamma). All twelve proper Euler and Tait-Bryan sequences are supported.

r <- robot_rotation(euler = c(0.3, -0.2, 0.1), sequence = "ZYX")
as_euler(r, "ZYX")
#> [1]  0.3 -0.2  0.1
as_euler(r, "XYZ")
#> [1]  0.1564195 -0.1600272  0.3226097
as_euler(r, "ZXZ")
#> [1] -0.8031300  0.2233075  1.1131718

At gimbal lock (pitch \pm\pi/2 for "ZYX"), the decomposition is not unique. The returned angles still reproduce the matrix:

r <- robot_rotation(euler = c(0.4, pi / 2, 0.1), sequence = "ZYX")
a <- as_euler(r, "ZYX")
a
#> [1] 0.300000 1.570796 0.000000
max(abs(robot_rotation(euler = a, sequence = "ZYX")$matrix - r$matrix))
#> [1] 1.110223e-16

URDF rpy attributes are fixed-axis roll, pitch, yaw, which equal the intrinsic "ZYX" angles in reverse order.

Axis-angle, rotation vectors and quaternions 

r <- robot_rotation(axis = c(1, 1, 0), angle = 2)
as_axis_angle(r)
#> $axis
#> [1] 0.7071068 0.7071068 0.0000000
#> 
#> $angle
#> [1] 2
as_rotvec(r)
#> [1] 1.414214 1.414214 0.000000
q <- robot_quaternion(r)
q
#> <robot_quaternion> w = 0.540302, (x, y, z) = (0.59501, 0.59501, 0)

Quaternions are scalar first and use the Hamilton product. Since q and -q represent the same rotation, the canonical form has w \ge 0.

qa <- robot_quaternion(robot_rotation(axis = c(0, 0, 1), angle = 0.5))
qb <- robot_quaternion(robot_rotation(axis = c(0, 1, 0), angle = 0.8))
qa * qb
#> <robot_quaternion> w = 0.892427, (x, y, z) = (-0.0963436, 0.377312, 0.227874)
quaternion_rotate(qa, c(1, 0, 0))
#> [1] 0.8775826 0.4794255 0.0000000
quaternion_distance(qa, qb)
#> [1] 0.9361988
quaternion_slerp(qa, qb, c(0, 0.5, 1))
#> [[1]]
#> <robot_quaternion> w = 0.968912, (x, y, z) = (0, 0, 0.247404)
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> <robot_quaternion> w = 0.971474, (x, y, z) = (0, 0.200167, 0.127169)
#> 
#> [[3]]
#> <robot_quaternion> w = 0.921061, (x, y, z) = (0, 0.389418, 0)

quaternion_slerp() follows the shortest arc and returns unit quaternions.

Rigid transformations

A pose T_{ab} \in SE(3) maps coordinates in frame b to frame a:

T_{ab} = \begin{pmatrix} R_{ab} & p_{ab} \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad p_a = R_{ab} p_b + p_{ab}.

Frames can be named so that mismatched compositions fail loudly:

T_world_base <- robot_pose(rotz(pi / 2), c(1, 0, 0), parent = "world", child = "base")
T_base_tool <- robot_pose(translation = c(0, 0, 0.5), parent = "base", child = "tool")
T_world_tool <- T_world_base * T_base_tool
T_world_tool
#> <robot_pose> SE(3) world <- tool
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4]
#> [1,]    0   -1    0  1.0
#> [2,]    1    0    0  0.0
#> [3,]    0    0    1  0.5
#> [4,]    0    0    0  1.0
robot_transform_point(T_world_tool, rbind(c(0, 0, 0), c(0.1, 0, 0)))
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3]
#> [1,]    1  0.0  0.5
#> [2,]    1  0.1  0.5
try(T_base_tool * T_world_base)
#> Error : Frame mismatch: left pose ends in 'tool' but right pose starts in 'world'.

Inverse and relative poses:

robot_inverse(T_world_base)
#> <robot_pose> SE(3) base <- world
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4]
#> [1,]    0    1    0    0
#> [2,]   -1    0    0    1
#> [3,]    0    0    1    0
#> [4,]    0    0    0    1
robot_relative_pose(T_world_base, T_world_tool)
#> <robot_pose> SE(3) base <- tool
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4]
#> [1,]    1    0    0  0.0
#> [2,]    0    1    0  0.0
#> [3,]    0    0    1  0.5
#> [4,]    0    0    0  1.0
robot_pose_distance(T_world_base, T_world_tool)
#> translation    rotation 
#>         0.5         0.0

Lie group tools

The exponential and logarithm maps connect rotations and poses to their tangent spaces. robotcompR uses series expansions near zero and dedicated branches near \pi, so round trips stay accurate in both regimes.

w <- c(0.1, -0.4, 0.3)
max(abs(so3_log(so3_exp(w)) - w))
#> [1] 0
w_pi <- c(0, 0, pi - 1e-9)
so3_log(so3_exp(w_pi))
#> [1] 0.000000 0.000000 3.141593
xi <- c(0.5, 0.2, -0.1, 0.3, 0.2, -0.4)  # linear part first
max(abs(se3_log(se3_exp(xi)) - xi))
#> [1] 1.110223e-16

The left Jacobian of SO(3) relates small tangent perturbations to perturbations of the rotation: \exp(\phi + \delta) \approx \exp(J_l(\phi)\delta)\exp(\phi).

phi <- c(0.4, -0.2, 0.7)
d <- c(1e-6, 0, 0)
lhs <- so3_exp(phi + d) %*% t(so3_exp(phi))
max(abs(so3_log(lhs) - so3_jacobian_left(phi) %*% d))
#> [1] 5.223193e-14

The adjoint maps twists between frames. With linear-first twists \xi = (v, \omega):

\mathrm{Ad}_T = \begin{pmatrix} R & [p]_\times R \\ 0 & R \end{pmatrix}. 

T <- robot_pose(rotz(0.3), c(1, 2, 0))
round(se3_adjoint(T), 4)
#>        [,1]    [,2] [,3]    [,4]    [,5] [,6]
#> [1,] 0.9553 -0.2955    0  0.0000  0.0000    2
#> [2,] 0.2955  0.9553    0  0.0000  0.0000   -1
#> [3,] 0.0000  0.0000    1 -1.6152  1.5464    0
#> [4,] 0.0000  0.0000    0  0.9553 -0.2955    0
#> [5,] 0.0000  0.0000    0  0.2955  0.9553    0
#> [6,] 0.0000  0.0000    0  0.0000  0.0000    1

Interpolating poses

robot_pose_interp() either interpolates translation linearly and rotation by slerp ("decoupled"), or moves along the constant twist joining the poses ("screw"). Both agree at the endpoints.

a <- robot_pose()
b <- robot_pose(rotz(pi / 2), c(1, 1, 0))
mid <- robot_pose_interp(a, b, 0.5, method = "decoupled")
pose_translation(mid)
#> [1] 0.5 0.5 0.0
mid_screw <- robot_pose_interp(a, b, 0.5, method = "screw")
pose_translation(mid_screw)
#> [1] 0.7071068 0.2928932 0.0000000

Planar rotations and poses 

so2_exp(pi / 3)
#>           [,1]       [,2]
#> [1,] 0.5000000 -0.8660254
#> [2,] 0.8660254  0.5000000
se2_exp(c(1, 0, pi / 2))
#>              [,1]          [,2]      [,3]
#> [1,] 6.123234e-17 -1.000000e+00 0.6366198
#> [2,] 1.000000e+00  6.123234e-17 0.6366198
#> [3,] 0.000000e+00  0.000000e+00 1.0000000
wrap_angle(c(3 * pi, -3 * pi / 2))
#> [1] -3.141593  1.570796
